differences.title: 1. EXECUTION MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Ansible executes tasks sequentially by pushing configurations from a control node to managed nodes via SSH or WinRM, making it imperative.
differences.rightDesc: Terraform defines desired state and calculates a plan to reach it. It then applies this plan, managing resources in a declarative way.

differences.title: 2. STATE MANAGEMENT
differences.leftDesc: Ansible doesn't maintain a persistent state file of managed resources, relying on idempotency of modules to ensure desired outcomes.
differences.rightDesc: Terraform uses a state file (e.g., `terraform.tfstate`) to map real-world resources to your configuration and track changes.

differences.title: 3. INFRASTRUCTURE PROVISIONING
differences.leftDesc: Primarily excels at configuring existing infrastructure, software installation, and application deployment through its task-based modules.
differences.rightDesc: Designed from the ground up for provisioning and managing entire infrastructure lifecycles across various cloud providers and services.

differences.title: 4. AGENT REQUIREMENT
differences.leftDesc: Connects to managed nodes via SSH (Linux/Unix) or WinRM (Windows) without requiring any pre-installed agent software.
differences.rightDesc: Typically operates agentlessly, using provider APIs to interact with cloud resources. Some specific use cases might involve agents.

differences.title: 5. IDEMPOTENCY
differences.leftDesc: Achieved through carefully written modules designed to be run multiple times without unintended side effects, ensuring a consistent end state.
differences.rightDesc: Intrinsic to resource definitions; Terraform ensures the current state matches the declared state by detecting drift and applying changes.

differences.title: 6. COMMUNITY & ECOSYSTEM
differences.leftDesc: Vast collection of community-contributed roles, playbooks, and modules available through Ansible Galaxy for rapid deployment.
differences.rightDesc: Extensive provider ecosystem and modules in the Terraform Registry enabling management of diverse cloud and SaaS services.

differences.title: 7. LEARNING CURVE
differences.leftDesc: YAML-based playbooks are generally considered more human-readable and easier to grasp initially, especially for sysadmins.
differences.rightDesc: HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) or JSON syntax, coupled with state management concepts, can present a steeper initial learning curve.
